name: Cylindrical Waves and a Cosmic String
description: Outside a straight cosmic string, cylindrical gravitational waves form a vacuum geometry whose angle deficit is larger far from the axis.
convention: The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu}=R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: For a circle around a positive tension cosmic string, the ratio of circumference to proper radius approaches a value below $2\pi$ as the radius tends to zero. The missing angle marks the string on the axis [gurtug_sakalli2003]. Cylindrical gravitational waves surround the string in a vacuum geometry [gurtug_sakalli2003, xanthopoulos1986cylindrical]. ¶ In cylindrical coordinates $(t,\rho,\phi,z)$, the line element is $ds^2=A(-dt^2+d\rho^2)+\rho^2X\,d\phi^2/Y+(Y/X)(dz-\omega\,d\phi)^2$ [gurtug_sakalli2003]. Here $A=\alpha^2X/(\tau^2+\sigma^2)$, $X=(1-p\tau)^2+q^2\sigma^2$, and $Y=p^2(1+\tau^2)+q^2(\sigma^2-1)$. The twist is $\omega=2q(\sigma^2-1)(1-p\tau)/(pY)$, with $q^2-p^2=1$. The auxiliary coordinates obey $t=\tau\sigma$ and $\rho^2=(1+\tau^2)(\sigma^2-1)$. ¶ At the axis the deficit is $2\pi(1-1/|\alpha p|)$ [gurtug_sakalli2003]. It vanishes when $|\alpha p|=1$, leaving a regular axis. Far from the axis at fixed time, the corresponding deficit is $2\pi(1-1/|\alpha q|)$ [gurtug_sakalli2003]. At fixed $t$ and $\rho$, the limit $p\to\infty$ with $\alpha p=k>1$ approaches the locally flat exterior of a straight string [gurtug_sakalli2003]. Scaling time and radius by $k$ leaves the angular factor $1/k^2$. ¶ Basilis C. Xanthopoulos obtained this solution in 1986 through a complex transformation of the Kerr metric [xanthopoulos1986rotating]. His family is of Petrov type D and has no curvature singularities [gurtug_sakalli2003, xanthopoulos1986cylindrical]. Athanasios Economou and Dimitri Tsoubelis found a broader family of cylindrical soliton waves, with Xanthopoulos's geometry as a subfamily [kleidis2010, economou_tsoubelis1988]. Xanthopoulos described the waves as nonradiating [garriga_verdaguer1987, xanthopoulos1986cylindrical]. At fixed time, the C-energy flux tends to zero far from the axis [gurtug_sakalli2003]. At null infinity, the waves carry a nonzero C-energy flux [kleidis2010]. ¶ Xanthopoulos interpreted the axis as a rotating cosmic string [xanthopoulos1986rotating]. Jiří Bičák, Joseph Katz, and Donald Lynden-Bell evaluated the Komar angular momentum and found it zero for this geometry [bicak_katz_lyndenbell2008]. The cross term in the line element couples the angular and longitudinal directions [gurtug_sakalli2003].

coordinates.convention: We use dimensionless coordinates $(\psi,\theta,\phi,z)$, with $\tau=\sinh\psi$ and $\sigma=\cosh\theta$. The axis is at $\theta=0$, where this polar chart ends. A dot denotes differentiation with respect to an affine parameter.

related.text: The conical exterior appears as $p\to\infty$ with $\alpha p=k>1$, after scaling time and radius by $k$ [gurtug_sakalli2003].
The waves fit the cylindrical metric with two polarisations; $|\alpha p|=1$ makes the axis regular [gurtug_sakalli2003].
Xanthopoulos obtained the cylindrical waves through a complex transformation of Kerr's metric [xanthopoulos1986rotating].
Einstein and Rosen's cylindrical waves have one polarisation; the waves around the string also have a crossed polarisation [gurtug_sakalli2003].
Spinning cosmic strings carry angular momentum. The Komar angular momentum of the cylindrical wave geometry is zero [bicak_katz_lyndenbell2008].
Garfinkle and Vachaspati's wave travels along a cosmic string. Xanthopoulos's waves have cylindrical fronts around the axis [garfinkle1990, gurtug_sakalli2003].
The inverse scattering construction leads to cylindrical soliton waves around a string, with Xanthopoulos's waves in a subfamily [kleidis2010].
